question: Explain the difference between stack and heap memory allocation.

key_points: Stack: stores local variables/function call frames; allocation/deallocation is automatic (LIFO) and very fast, tied to function scope
Heap: used for dynamically allocated memory whose lifetime isn't tied to a function call; allocation/deallocation is manual (or GC-managed) and slower
Stack memory is limited (stack overflow on deep/infinite recursion); heap is larger but fragmentable and requires explicit management or a garbage collector
Explains why heap access is generally slower than stack access due to less predictable memory layout/locality
reference_solution.sample_answer: Stack memory is used for local variables and function call frames; it's allocated and freed automatically in last-in-first-out order as functions are called and return, which makes it very fast, but it's limited in size — deep or infinite recursion causes a stack overflow. Heap memory is for dynamically allocated data whose lifetime isn't tied to a particular function call; it has to be explicitly managed, either manually (malloc/free in C) or automatically via a garbage collector in languages like Java or Python, and it's generally slower to access than the stack due to less predictable memory layout and potential fragmentation, though it offers much more available space and flexible lifetimes.

follow_up_hint: Ask what causes a stack overflow and how it differs from a heap 'out of memory' error.

question: What is a memory leak, and how can it occur in a garbage-collected language like Java or JavaScript?

key_points: A memory leak is memory that's no longer needed by the program but is never freed, causing memory usage to grow over time

In a GC language, this happens when an object is still reachable via some reference chain (even accidentally), so the garbage collector can't reclaim it even though it's logically 'dead' to the program
Common causes: forgotten event listeners/subscriptions that are never unregistered, a growing cache/collection with no eviction, closures unintentionally holding references to large objects
In JS specifically: detached DOM nodes still referenced by JS variables, global variables accumulating data, timers/intervals never cleared
reference_solution.sample_answer: A memory leak is memory that the program no longer actually needs but never releases, causing usage to grow unbounded over time. In a garbage-collected language, this doesn't mean 'forgetting to free memory' the way it does in C — instead, it happens when an object remains reachable through some reference chain even though it's logically no longer needed, so the garbage collector correctly determines it's still 'in use' and can't reclaim it. Common causes include event listeners or subscriptions that are registered but never unregistered, keeping the subscriber alive indefinitely; an ever-growing cache or collection with no eviction policy; or closures that unintentionally capture and hold onto references to large objects longer than needed. In JavaScript specifically, forgetting to clear a setInterval, or holding a JS reference to a DOM node that's been removed from the document, are classic leak patterns.

follow_up_hint: Ask them how they'd actually diagnose a memory leak in a running application (heap snapshots, profiling tools).

question: Explain reference counting versus mark-and-sweep garbage collection.

key_points: Reference counting: each object tracks how many references point to it; when the count hits zero, it's immediately freed
Reference counting weakness: can't detect/collect cyclic references (two objects referencing each other but unreachable from the rest of the program) without extra handling

Mark-and-sweep: periodically traces all objects reachable from a set of 'roots' (marking them live), then frees ('sweeps') everything unmarked — correctly handles cycles since unreachable cycles simply aren't marked

Trade-off: reference counting has more consistent, immediate overhead per assignment but simpler/more predictable pauses; mark-and-sweep can handle cycles but introduces a 'stop-the-world' pause (or more complex incremental/concurrent variants) during collection
reference_solution.sample_answer: Reference counting tracks, for each object, how many references currently point to it, and frees the object immediately once that count drops to zero. Its major weakness is that it can't reclaim cyclic references on its own — if object A references B and B references A, but nothing else references either of them, their counts never reach zero even though they're both genuinely unreachable garbage, so a cycle detector has to be layered on top. Mark-and-sweep instead periodically starts from a set of root references, traces and marks everything reachable as 'live', then frees everything else that wasn't marked, which correctly handles cycles since an unreachable cycle just never gets marked. The trade-off is reference counting has small, continuous overhead spread across every reference assignment but reasonably predictable behavior, while mark-and-sweep correctly handles cycles but traditionally introduces a noticeable 'stop-the-world' pause during collection, which is why modern collectors use incremental or concurrent variants to reduce that pause.

follow_up_hint: Ask which garbage collection strategy Python's CPython actually uses (hint: it uses both — reference counting plus a cycle detector).

question: What is a dangling pointer, and how do modern languages prevent this class of bug?

key_points: A dangling pointer references memory that has already been freed/deallocated; using it (dereferencing, freeing again) is undefined behavior — can cause crashes or corrupt unrelated data

Common cause in C/C++: freeing memory but keeping a pointer to it (a 'use-after-free' bug) and later dereferencing that stale pointer, or returning a pointer to a stack-local variable that no longer exists after the function returns
Garbage-collected languages prevent this by not freeing an object's memory as long as any reference to it still exists, making dangling references impossible by construction
Rust prevents this at compile time via its ownership/borrow checker, without needing runtime garbage collection at all
reference_solution.sample_answer: A dangling pointer points to memory that has already been freed or deallocated; dereferencing it is undefined behavior that can crash the program or, worse, silently read or corrupt memory that's since been reused for something else — this is the classic 'use-after-free' bug in languages like C and C++. It can also happen by returning a pointer to a local stack variable, which ceases to exist once the function returns. Garbage-collected languages sidestep this entirely by never freeing an object's memory while any reference to it is still reachable, so a dangling reference simply can't exist. Rust takes a different, compile-time approach: its ownership and borrow checker statically proves that no reference can outlive the data it points to, catching what would be a dangling pointer as a compile error, without needing any runtime garbage collector at all.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to explain, at a high level, how Rust's borrow checker prevents a reference from outliving its owner.
